evidence.title: Payne baronets
evidence.text: The Payne Baronetcy, of St Christopher's in the West Indies, was a title in the Baronetage of Great Britain.

evidence.title: Payne baronets
evidence.text: It was created on 31 October 1737 for Charles Payne.

evidence.title: Payne baronets
evidence.text: According to some sources that title became extinct on the death of the second Baronet, Sir Gillis Payne, in 1801.

evidence.title: Payne baronets
evidence.text: Sir Gillis was in a relationship with a farmer's daughter, Maria Keeling.

evidence.title: Payne baronets
evidence.text: They apparently married in 1761 although several children had been born before this date.

evidence.title: Payne baronets
evidence.text: Peter Payne was the eldest son born after the marriage and would normally have succeeded in the title.

evidence.title: Payne baronets
evidence.text: However, he allowed his eldest brother John Payne to assume the title, although John was illegitimate.

evidence.title: Payne baronets
evidence.text: John died in 1803 when his son Charles assumed the title.

evidence.title: Payne baronets
evidence.text: However, in 1828 Peter Payne raised the question in the courts over who was the rightful baronet.

evidence.title: Payne baronets
evidence.text: The Court of Chancery declared that he was the rightful heir to his father, but this was overturned by the Lord Chancellor in 1829.

evidence.title: Payne baronets
evidence.text: Nonetheless, during his lifetime Sir Peter was universally acknowledged as a baronet.

evidence.title: Payne baronets
evidence.text: Most reference books on the British nobility and baronetage include the title, although they describe it as being in dispute between rival branches of the family.

evidence.title: Payne baronets
evidence.text: Charles Robert Salusbury Payne, the supposed sixth Baronet, appears to have discontinued the claim around 1900.
